title: Going shopping
goal: Buy things, ask about prices, pay without cash, and understand the phrases a Swedish cashier rattles off at top speed.
bekal: set phrases for shops, cafés and the checkout
*finns det…?* — the way to ask whether something is available

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På ICA och på caféet
dialogs.intro: Thursday afternoon. Dian is shopping at ICA before stopping by the campus café with Oskar.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Excuse me, is there any rice here?

lines.speaker: Personalen:
lines.text: Ja, i gång fyra, bredvid pastan.
lines.id: Yes, in aisle four, next to the pasta.
lines.literal: yes, in aisle four, beside pasta-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Tack. Och vad kostar den här osten?
lines.id: Thanks. And how much is this cheese?
lines.literal: thanks. and what costs the here cheese-the?

lines.speaker: Personalen:
lines.text: Sextionio kronor kilot. Den är på extrapris den här veckan.
lines.id: Sixty-nine kronor a kilo. It's on special offer this week.
lines.literal: sixty-nine kronor kilo-the. it is on extra-price the here week-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Då tar jag en bit. Var betalar man?
lines.id: Then I'll take a piece. Where do I pay?
lines.literal: then take I a piece. where pays one?

lines.speaker: Personalen:
lines.text: Vid självutcheckningen, eller i kassa två.
lines.id: At the self-checkout, or at checkout two.
lines.literal: at self-out-checking-the, or in checkout two.

lines.speaker: Kassören:
lines.text: Hej! Vill du ha kvitto? Och har du ICA-kort?
lines.id: Hi! Do you want a receipt? And do you have an ICA card?
lines.literal: hi! want you have receipt? and have you ICA-card?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej tack, inget kvitto. Och nej, jag har inget kort.
lines.id: No thanks, no receipt. And no, I don't have a card.
lines.literal: no thanks, no receipt. and no, I have no card.

lines.speaker: Kassören:
lines.text: Det blir tvåhundrafemton kronor. Kort eller Swish?
lines.id: That'll be two hundred and fifteen kronor. Card or Swish?
lines.literal: it becomes two-hundred-fifteen kronor. card or Swish?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Och på caféet sen — vill du ha en kaffe och en bulle?
lines.id: And at the café later — would you like a coffee and a bun?
lines.literal: and at café-the later — want you have a coffee and a bun?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Gärna. Men den här gången bjuder jag.
lines.id: I'd love to. But this time it's my treat.
lines.literal: gladly. but the here time-the treat I.

notes: **Finns det…?** is how you ask whether something is available: "is there…? / are there…?". *Finns* comes from *att finnas* (to exist, to be found), and it always goes with *det*, however many things you mean: *Finns det ris?*, *Finns det billiga hotell?* Unlike English, you don't switch between "is there" and "are there". The same pattern works for telling: *Det finns ett apotek vid torget.*

**Det blir…** is the cashier phrase you will hear most — literally "it becomes…", meaning "that'll be…". The verb *bli* (to become) turns up in lots of unexpected places: *det blir bra* (it'll be fine), *det blir kallt* (it's going to be cold), *vi blir fem* (there will be five of us).

**Swish** is a phone-number-based payment app used by almost everyone in Sweden. Together with cards, it has almost completely replaced cash: many shops, cafés and even churches put up signs saying *Vi tar inte kontanter* (we don't accept cash). Arriving in Sweden with nothing but banknotes is the quickest way to go hungry.

**Extrapris** means sale price; other words worth recognizing on the shelves: *rea* (sale), *erbjudande* (offer), *stammis* (regular customer), *bäst före* (best before). That last one is not the expiry date — for that, the label says *sista förbrukningsdag*.

**Jag bjuder** means "it's my treat". The verb *bjuda* also means "to invite": *jag bjuder dig på middag* can mean inviting someone to dinner and paying for it. Bear in mind that splitting the bill is the standard habit in Sweden — offering to pay is a special gesture, not automatic politeness.

**Inget kvitto** uses *inget*, not *inte*. To negate a **noun**, Swedish uses *ingen/inget/inga* — the form follows the gender and number of the noun, just like an adjective: *ingen bok*, *inget kort*, *inga pengar*. English does the same with "no" (no book, no card, no money) — Swedish just has three shapes of it.

grammars.title: Ingen, inget, inga
body: You already use *inte* to negate a sentence. To negate a noun, there is a separate family of words:
after: The last column shows that there are always two ways to say the same thing — just as English has "I have no car" and "I don't have a car". The *ingen* form is shorter and more common in simple sentences; the *inte någon* form is required when there is a helper verb: *Jag kan **inte** hitta **någon** nyckel* — not *jag kan ingen nyckel hitta*.
**Ingenting** (nothing) and **ingen** (nobody) stand on their own without a noun. Their positive cousins: *någonting/något* (something) and *någon* (somebody).

grammars.title: Checkout phrases, word by word

head: What you hear
Meaning
Your answer
rows: Ja tack. / Nej, jag vill ha…
Do you have a membership card?
Have a nice rest of your day!

after: These phrases come out very fast, with hardly a pause, because cashiers say them hundreds of times a day. Don't panic: you can get through an entire Swedish checkout with three words — *hej*, *nej tack*, *tack*.
**Detsamma!** means "you too!" and is the standard reply to any good wishes. Alternatives: *tack detsamma* or *du med*.

blocks.text: **Ett hekto** (100 grams) is a unit still alive and well in Sweden, though most other countries have dropped it. At the meat and cheese counter, people order *två hekto skinka* (200 grams of ham). If you say grams, the staff will still understand — but *hekto* is what you will hear.

blocks.title: Phrases you will say
items: **Jag skulle vilja ha…** — I would like… (the politest form in shops and restaurants)
**Finns det…?** — Is there…? / Do you have…?
**Har ni den här i storlek M?** — Do you have this in a medium?
**Kan jag få prova?** — Can I try it on?
**Vad kostar det?** — How much is it?
**Det är för dyrt.** — It's too expensive.
**Jag tittar bara, tack.** — I'm just looking, thanks.

head: Svenska
English
rows: I'll have the dish of the day.
Could we have the check, please?

blocks.text: **Dagens rätt** — often written just *dagens* — is the fixed-price lunch that almost every Swedish restaurant serves on weekdays, usually from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. It costs far less than the dinner menu and usually includes salad, bread and coffee. It is the cheapest way to eat out in Sweden.

**Påtår** means your second cup of coffee, and in many cafés it is **free** — ask *ingår påtår?* (is a refill included?). English "refill" only gets you halfway: Swedish has a dedicated word for that second cup, which tells you a lot about the place of coffee in Swedish culture.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 12
items: Give the three forms of five adjectives: stor, ny, liten, gammal, billig.
Then use them in shopping sentences: *Har ni en billigare tröja?*, *Den här är för dyr*, *Jag vill ha den lilla påsen*.
Finally, ask the price of five things around you using *Vad kostar…?* and answer with Swedish numbers.
